title: The All-In Podcast Flags Red Flags in Anthropic's IPO. What Everyday Investors Should Know - 24/7 Wall St.
content: The All-In hosts spotted numbers in Anthropic's Investor Day presentation that raised serious questions, and the valuation multiple they flagged would demand a lot from buyers who show up on day one. Here is what retirement investors and Microsoft shareholders… Anthropic’s planned IPO now has a vocal panel of skeptics. On the October 17, 2026 episode of the All-In Podcast, CoreWeave Crash, AI Trade Cracks, Anthropic IPO Red Flags, Bill Gates Doomer, the hosts said Anthropic plans to go public around Thanksgiving and that its Investor Day numbers drew mixed reactions. The discussion gives a useful checklist to retirement savers thinking about a hot AI listing and to holders of Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction). The All-In Podcast hosts said the market-implied probability that Anthropic goes public this year had fallen to 74%, down from 95% in early September. That figure reflects trader expectations on timing. Investor day figures read on the show included Q3 revenue of $16.8 billion, net revenue retention of 900%, an adjusted gross margin of 85% and an adjusted operating margin of 11%. One host added, “No word on how the adjustments were calculated.” Another noted that participants reportedly signed NDAs: “I don’t know if you can completely trust what’s floating around X here. I think we’ll find out in due course.” Chamath Palihapitiya called the growth remarkable: “I found the revenue breathtaking. $16.8 billion in a quarter for a three-year-old company is just ridiculous.” He also argued Anthropic should raise $200 billion to $250 billion at a lower valuation to secure compute. A host on the All-In Podcast described “a very big IPO, 30 times price-to-sales ratio.” A price-to-sales ratio divides a company’s market value by its annual revenue. At the All-In Podcast’s 30x multiple, buyers pay $30 for every $1 of annual sales. The higher the multiple, the longer revenue must compound, and margins must expand to justify the price, and any slowdown tends to hit high-priced stocks hardest. For perspective, Microsoft trades at 11.74 times trailing sales with an operating margin of about 46.8%. Hot IPOs often price with a small float so that first-day demand can push shares well above the offer, and open-market buyers pay that premium. Insiders usually face a lockup, and its expiration can add supply months later. Index funds may also have to buy once a stock becomes eligible, which can make retirement accounts buyers by default. Once an S-1 lands on the SEC’s EDGAR system, focus on audited revenue, how “adjusted” margins are defined, compute commitments, customer concentration, and use of proceeds. One host noted that an IPO next month would reveal the actual figures. Microsoft already books results tied to Anthropic. In fiscal Q4 2026, it recorded a $3.20 billion gain on its Anthropic investment, helping non-GAAP diluted EPS reach $4.74 against a $4.24 consensus, per its earnings release filed with the SEC. It also holds roughly a 27% stake in rival OpenAI, valued at about $135 billion. A public Anthropic price would re-mark that kind of exposure daily. Sentiment travels, too. As one All-In host said, “Anytime there’s negative news on the big labs, everybody in the supply chain gets hit with that.” That supply chain, the power, cooling, and networking vendors behind the data centers, is where a lot of the quieter AI money is being made (we highlighted seven such companies in a free report on AI infrastructure suppliers). A CNBC Fast Money panelist warned on October 14 that “if Anthropic goes public, it goes much less than where it’s trading right now.” On Bloomberg Businessweek, Mandeep Singh said hyperscalers should “shine” while “the lab side seems to be incrementally slowing down because of open source pressure.” Microsoft’s scale offers a buffer. Its AI business exceeded a $37 billion annualized run rate in fiscal Q3, Azure passed $100 billion in fiscal 2026 revenue, and full-year capex reached $115.95 billion. Shares sit near $530, up 10.29% year to date and 2.66% over the past year. Microsoft’s next earnings report is nearing this week, and an Anthropic S-1 would follow if the Thanksgiving timeline holds. Watch whether audited filings confirm the investor day figures and whether Microsoft’s capex and AI demand commentary stabilizes the broader trade. title: Microsoft offers around 60,000 employees voluntary buyouts - Yahoo Finance UK
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results US tech giant Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to employees around the globe, its chief people officer announced on Monday. In a memo sent to staff, Amy Coleman called the "Voluntary Exit Offer" an "important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter." The offer will be made available to employees on select teams across the US, Canada, India and the United Kingdom "at level 70 and below," meaning some senior staff could be included. "This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources," the memo continued. It added that eligible employees would receive an email with a link to their offers in the coming hours. In July, Microsoft announced it was eliminating around 4,800 roles, or roughly 2.1% of its global workforce at the time, as the company sought to shift its focus and cut costs as the AI era continues to take hold. Those cuts mostly affected the firm's commercial and Xbox gaming divisions. Microsoft also offered some staff the option to retire early this year. The company has said that more than 30% of those eligible for the early retirement scheme chose to participate and that it would "continue exploring similar approaches in the future." title: Microsoft’s Copilot, Azure Demand Signals Stronger AI Monetization: Analyst - TradingView
content: Microsoft Corp. MSFT remains in focus as investors assess whether accelerating AI adoption across Azure and Copilot can support revenue growth while the company continues funding its infrastructure buildout. BNP Paribas analyst Stefan Slowinski maintained an Outperform rating on Microsoft and a $604 price forecast on Monday, implying about 15% upside from the Oct. 23 reference price of $524.50. Slowinski said feedback from Microsoft’s Frontier Tour showed rising enterprise interest in Copilot, with more customers moving from pilot programs to companywide deployments. Slowinski expects the new E7 bundle and expanded agent capabilities to support broader adoption. He reiterated his view that Microsoft’s new consumption-based pricing could add about 1 percentage point to Microsoft 365 Commercial Cloud growth by fiscal fourth quarter. He also highlighted rising customer interest in standardizing on Microsoft’s broader software stack to capture AI benefits and reduce spending on overlapping providers. Examples include migrations from Power BI to Fabric, GitLab to GitHub and VMware environments to Azure services. Slowinski expects Azure growth to strengthen further. He cited buy-side expectations of roughly 46% growth for fiscal first quarter, above Microsoft’s 44%-45% guidance. He also sees additional acceleration potential in fiscal second quarter as OpenAI revenue sharing increases following the launch of GPT-6 Astra. Slowinski said Microsoft is strengthening AI monetization across Azure, Foundry, Fabric and Copilot, while its commitment to remain free-cash-flow positive supports its ability to fund investment internally. He views Copilot and Foundry as competitive differentiators, particularly against Amazon.com Inc. AMZN Amazon Web Services, while noting that Alphabet Inc. GOOG GOOGL Google Cloud remains more aggressive with migration incentives. Slowinski considers Microsoft’s roughly 24-times calendar 2027 P/E reasonable given its accelerating revenue growth and expanding AI monetization opportunity. content: Microsoft Corp.(MSFT) is launching a workforce reduction initiative, extending voluntary buyout offers to approximately 60,000 employees, Bloomberg reported. According to the report, the move is designed to control operational expenditures and retool personnel capabilities to match the rapidly expanding artificial intelligence landscape. A company spokesperson told Bloomberg that the buyout option applies to personnel at the vice president level and below within designated teams across the United States, Canada, India, and the United Kingdom. However, specific operational units—including certain groups tied to data centers, sales, and marketing—are excluded from the current round. Chief People Officer Amy Coleman addressed staff in an internal memorandum on Monday, noting that the initiative provides a structured exit path with corporate backing for those contemplating a career shift outside the company. Participating workers will receive benefits mirroring standard severance terms. Microsoft's total headcount stood at roughly 223,000 at the close of June. Total employee figures have remained relatively flat since 2022. While Microsoft previously executed a voluntary buyout targeting retirement-age staff in July, which saw over 30% of the 8,750 eligible workers accept, company representatives expect a significantly smaller proportion of personnel to take up the new, broader proposal. Microsoft is not alone in its efforts to adjust its workforce to accommodate the AI boom. Competitors have similarly reduced headcounts to redirect capital into heavy-duty data infrastructure. Meta Platforms Inc. has trimmed its staff significantly from its late 2022 peak, while Google implemented voluntary buyout initiatives across several divisions. Tech executives increasingly emphasize a faster operational tempo and an explicit commitment to rapid technological change. Coleman emphasized in her memo that the buyout framework gives individual Microsoft divisions an alternative way to adjust their labor pools to shifting corporate demands. Speaking on the Bankless podcast, Howell, a global liquidity expert and the Managing Director at GL Indexes, said his base case was still that global liquidity will not bottom until the second half of 2027. However, he said Bitcoin’s recent stability could be an early signal of a turn. “If you get Bitcoin holding above 70,000, if you see more evidence that bank reserves are being managed and maybe being pushed up, then I would powerfully change my view and expect to see liquidity picking up,” Howell said. In that case, Bitcoin could be signaling the early stages of “another two to three year bull market,” he added. Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve will announce its policy decision on Wednesday, with third-quarter (Q3) GDP and September inflation data due Thursday morning. Here are three charts to track as the market unfolds this week. Microsoft and Alphabet shares have taken divergent paths since July, and their upcoming earnings reports will give investors another chance to assess their growth and spending plans. Microsoft has led the group in the chart above, while Alphabet and semiconductor stocks tied to its infrastructure spending have lagged. The question for investors is no longer simply whether demand for AI is growing. They also want to know how much companies must spend to capture that demand, how quickly the investments will generate returns, and how they plan to finance the buildout. Meta Platforms (META) offered a recent example of how quickly sentiment can change. The company beat revenue estimates last Wednesday, but its shares fell almost 8% on Thursday after it unveiled a new class of nonvoting Class C shares. Microsoft is expected to report earnings per share (EPS) of $4.72 and revenue of $90.75 billion, as per Koyfin data. Investors will be watching Azure growth numbers and whether demand can support the company’s infrastructure investments. Microsoft guided in July to Azure growth of about 45%. Amazon’s AWS business faces a similar test when the company reports Thursday. Wall Street is expecting EPS of $1.96 on revenue of $202.20 billion. The growth of its cloud business will also be in focus. MSFT stock edged 0.5% higher in premarket trade on Monday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the firm has trended in ‘bearish’ territory over the past week. Meanwhile, AMZN stock edged 0.3% higher, with retail sentiment around the shares falling to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ territory over the past day. Meanwhile, Alphabet had faced scrutiny after raising its capital expenditure outlook in July, despite beating earnings estimates. Another jump in spending could test investors’ willingness to fund the AI buildout. The market is expecting EPS of $2.97 on revenue of $127.83 billion. GOOGL stock moved 0.4% higher in premarket trade and saw retail sentiment on Stocktwits around the company flip to ‘bullish’ from ‘bearish’ over the past week. South Korea’s SK Hynix (SKHY) is expected to report its third quarter results Tuesday night. Wall Street consensus estimates on Koyfin peg revenue to come in at $74.81 billion. While analysts expect another record quarter, investors will be looking out for management’s outlook as the more important variable. A substantial shareholder-return plan could provide a reason to own the stock beyond the AI growth story. Second, more cautious comments on high-bandwidth memory pricing or demand in 2027 could reinforce concerns that current earnings are difficult to sustain. Lastly, competition from China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and any commentary on the same could provide the market with greater visibility into demand in 2027 and 2028. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the firm remained in ‘bullish’ territory over the past day. A more hawkish message could push short-term yields higher, while a statement that leaves the door open to easing could send them lower. title: Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy Microsoft Stock - The Motley Fool
content: Earnings jumped 22% last fiscal year. Why would I still want the stock around 12% cheaper? Microsoft (MSFT +1.54%) closed at a record $543.45 on Oct. 13, and it hasn't moved far since. Shares trade near $530 as of this writing, about 2% off the high. Microsoft posts results for the fiscal first quarter of 2027 (the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026) after the market closes on Wednesday, Oct. 28. The company has earned a good chunk of that climb. Microsoft's adjusted earnings per share jumped 22% for fiscal 2026, which ended June 30. But at today's price, shares cost about 31 times those earnings. It's a steep price for a business whose own guidance suggests slower growth right as its capital spending keeps rising. I'd buy the stock at about $465 a share, roughly 12% under where it trades now. Microsoft's fiscal 2026 was impressive by nearly any measure. Revenue grew 18% to $331.8 billion, and operating income climbed 21% to $155.2 billion. Non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share, which strip out the effect of Microsoft's investments in OpenAI, increased 22% to $17.28. And the pace held up all year, with adjusted earnings per share up 23% year over year in both the first and fourth quarters of fiscal 2026. But the stock price already reflects much of that. With shares around $530, Microsoft trades at about 31 times its fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings. On reported earnings of $17.95 per share, it's about 30. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,742,263 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. The price-to-earnings ratio for the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.70%) on its reported earnings is about 26. The premium is easier to defend when earnings rise 22% a year. And management's forecast for the September quarter suggests growth is slowing, at least a little. Microsoft sees revenue between $89.85 billion and $90.95 billion, cost of revenue between $29.6 billion and $29.8 billion, and operating expenses between $16.8 billion and $16.9 billion. At these levels, operating income would climb around 14% to 17% from the year-ago quarter's $38.0 billion. This compares to year-over-year growth of 24%, 21%, 20%, and 18% over the four quarters of fiscal 2026. In short, operating income growth has slowed every quarter for a year, and the guidance shows it slowing again. The spending is the bigger reason I want a discount. Cash from operations grew a strong 34% in fiscal 2026, to about $183 billion. But Microsoft also spent almost $116 billion on additions to property and equipment, so free cash flow dipped about 6% to roughly $67 billion. What's more, management expects capital expenditures of about $175 billion in calendar 2026. "[W]e expect to remain free cash flow positive in FY27," chief financial officer Amy Hood said on Microsoft's earnings call in July. It's arguably a low bar -- Microsoft produced around $67 billion in free cash flow last fiscal year. My buy price starts with the $17.28 Microsoft earned per share last fiscal year on an adjusted basis. I'd pay a price-to-earnings multiple of around 27 on that number, which comes out to about $465 a share. At that price, Microsoft's price-to-earnings ratio on reported earnings would be about 26, on par with the S&P 500's. I think paying around the market's valuation multiple is fair for a business whose earnings growth looks set to cool toward the mid-teens as its spending keeps climbing. Shares last closed under $465 on July 31, two days after the company's fiscal fourth-quarter report pushed the stock sharply higher. The Oct. 28 report might shift my price in two ways. The first is earnings. Because my price is linked to trailing adjusted earnings per share, every strong quarter lifts it. Management's guidance suggests operating income growth of a bit over 15% at the midpoint. If adjusted earnings per share gained 15% from the year-ago period's $4.13, trailing adjusted earnings per share would reach around $17.90, and my buy price would rise to about $483. The second is Azure, Microsoft's cloud computing platform. As I wrote earlier this month, I think the stock needs Azure's growth to stay above 40%. If Azure falls short, or if free cash flow keeps dropping, I'd want to pay a lower price-to-earnings ratio than 27, and my buy price would fall with it. Would I buy Microsoft stock before Oct. 28? Not at roughly $530. Sure, a strong report might raise my buy price, and shares may never drop as low as $465. But at about 31 times adjusted earnings, I think the stock already reflects most of the good news. I'd consider buying closer to $465.
